outcome: A complete proof for every degree n ≥ 2 was posted on ProofAtlas by Lech Mazur (dated 2 Aug 2026 by its revision log, 5 Aug 2026 on the PDF and public version) with the credited role of OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro; Terence Tao digested it on 12 Aug 2026 and a Lean 4 formalization of Tao's version exists (teorth/sendov, built against Lean toolchains v4.33.1 to v4.35.0 with the stated theorem and only the standard axioms), but the author's own ProofAtlas pages call the manuscript a 'proof candidate' with independent specialist certification still pending, and I found no named human referee report, so the result is claimed and Lean-checked for the stated theorem but not accepted by an independent expert.
problem_asks: Sendov's conjecture, part by part, from the statement alone. (a) For every integer degree n ≥ 2: a universal claim over all degrees. (b) For every complex polynomial p of that degree whose zeros all lie in the closed unit disk |z| ≤ 1. (c) For every zero a of p (each root considered in turn). (d) There exists a critical point ζ of p, meaning a zero of p′, with |ζ − a| ≤ 1: a closed bound at the constant 1. The constant is sharp, since p(z) = z^n − 1 has every critical point at 0 and distance exactly 1 from each root, so the bound cannot be lowered. The statement is a single conjecture; its only parts are these quantifiers and the closed constant 1.

events.what_happened: Zalman Rubinstein's paper 'On a problem of Ilyeff' (1968): for zeros on the unit circle |a| = 1, a critical point lies within distance 1 in every degree, and for interior zeros in degrees 3 and 4. Identified from a search snippet of the Pacific Journal record and from the Lean package documentation, which calls the classification 'Rubinstein's 1968 theorem'. Not opened in full, and the snippet-to-record mapping is not confirmed.
events.delivers: Sendov for zeros on the unit circle in every degree, and the full statement for degrees 3 and 4 (interior zeros included), per the snippet and the Lean documentation.
events.remains: Interior zeros (0 ≤ |a| < 1) for every degree n ≥ 5.
events.direction: Confirms the conjecture in the restricted cases it covers.

events.what_happened: Meir and Sharma's 1969 partial result. The Wikipedia page I opened confirms only the 1969 date; a Wikipedia search snippet says it covers polynomials with n < 6. The paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Sendov for polynomials of degree n < 6 (per a search snippet of Wikipedia; not confirmed from the paper).
events.remains: Degrees n ≥ 6.
events.direction: Confirms the conjecture for low degrees.

events.what_happened: Johnny E. Brown, 'On the Ilieff–Sendov conjecture', Pacific J. Math. volume 135 (1988), proving the conjecture for polynomials of arbitrary degree with at most four distinct zeros. Known only from a search-result summary of the Pacific J. Math. record; not opened. Wikipedia as I read it dates a Brown partial result to 1991, which I could not reconcile.
events.delivers: Sendov for arbitrary degree when the polynomial has at most four distinct zeros (per the search-result summary).
events.remains: Polynomials with five or more distinct zeros in degrees beyond those already covered.

checked_by.who: Pacific Journal of Mathematics (journal of record)

events.direction: Confirms the conjecture in a restricted class (at most four distinct zeros).

events.what_happened: Johnny Brown and Guangping Xiang, 'Proof of the Sendov conjecture for polynomials of degree at most eight', J. Math. Anal. Appl. 232(2): 272–292 (1999), DOI 10.1006/jmaa.1999.6267 per a search summary. The Wikipedia and MathWorld pages I opened both record the degree-at-most-eight result. Per a search summary of a Purdue dissertation, Brown gave an independent proof for n ≤ 7 in 1997. The paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Sendov for all polynomials of degree at most 8; per the dissertation summary, also for arbitrary degree with at most eight distinct zeros and degree n ≥ 11.
events.remains: All polynomials of degree 9 and above, except the restricted class noted above.

checked_by.who: Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications (journal of record)

events.direction: Confirms the conjecture for degree at most 8.

events.what_happened: Gerald Schmieder, 'A proof of Sendov's conjecture' (arXiv math/0206173). The abstract, read in full, says only 'A proof of Sendov's conjecture is given.' It was revised eight times (v8 on 3 Jul 2003) and is not marked withdrawn on its abstract page. Per a search summary of Sendov's 2005 lecture notes (not opened), the eight arXiv proofs of 2002–2003 were not correct, and J. Borcea identified weak points; I did not locate Borcea's paper.
events.delivers: Claims a full proof of the conjecture, for all degrees.
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim held; the claim has been described by a secondary source as incorrect.
events.doubts: Per a search summary of Sendov's 2005 lecture notes (not opened), the 2002–2003 arXiv proofs by Schmieder 'are not correct', and J. Borcea identified weak points and argued the variational method does not apply. Not confirmed from the paper or Borcea's text.
events.direction: Claims to confirm the conjecture in full.

events.what_happened: Michael J. Miller, 'Unexpected local extrema for the Sendov conjecture' (arXiv math/0505424). Per a search summary (arXiv page not opened): gives sufficient conditions for certain polynomials built from integrals of (w − a)^(n−3)(w² + bw + c) to be locally extremal, finds such examples in degrees 8, 9, 12–15, 19, 20 and 26, and notes that maximising the distance d(P) over all locally extremal polynomials would settle the conjecture. Published in J. Math. Anal. Appl. 2008 per a bibliographic record.
events.revisions: Per search summary: v1 May 2005 (one degree-8 example); later versions added further degrees; last revised Aug 2007.
events.delivers: Partial: locally extremal examples in specific degrees; no proof of the conjecture.
events.remains: The conjecture in every degree; the locally extremal approach is said to need a global maximisation step.
events.direction: Partial progress toward the conjecture; does not resolve it.

events.what_happened: Zaizhao Meng, 'On the Sendov conjecture and the critical points of polynomials' (arXiv 1303.2279, 10 Mar 2013). The abstract reads: 'we obtain new results on the critical points of a polynomial' and 'We discuss the Sendov conjecture for polynomials of degree nine.' Read from the abstract page only.
events.revisions: v1 only.
events.delivers: Unclear from the abstract: 'discusses' the conjecture for degree nine; does not claim a full proof for that degree. Read from the abstract only.
events.remains: Unclear; the full text was not read.
events.doubts: Scope unclear from the abstract. The same author posted a full degree-nine claim in 2017 (see the next event).
events.direction: Unclear; partial at most.

events.what_happened: Dégot's 2014 result, as described in Chalebgwa's 2018 abstract (which I opened): for each a in (0,1) there is an integer N such that for any polynomial of degree greater than N with P(a) = 0 and all zeros in the unit disk, the disk |z − a| ≤ 1 contains a critical point. Dégot's own paper was not opened.
events.delivers: For zeros a in the open interval (0,1) only, and only for polynomials of sufficiently high degree (threshold N(a) depends on a).
events.remains: Zeros near 0 or near the unit circle; all degrees below the threshold; zeros outside (0,1).
events.direction: Confirms the conjecture for a restricted class of zeros in high degree.

events.what_happened: Zaizhao Meng, 'Proof of the Sendov conjecture for polynomials of degree nine' (arXiv 1705.07235, 20 May 2017). The abstract reads: 'In this paper, we prove the Sendov conjecture for polynomials of degree nine. We use a new idea to obtain new upper bound for the σ-sum to zeros of the polynomial.' No journal reference and no comments on the abstract page.
events.revisions: v1 20 May 2017; v2 22 Dec 2017; v3 17 May 2018 (the version shown).
events.delivers: Claims the full conjecture for polynomials of degree nine only (n = 9).
events.remains: All degrees other than nine; the stated restriction is degree 9.
events.doubts: No published venue or third-party review on the abstract page. The claim's correctness was not checked. Tao's 2020 paper and the 2026 accounts treat degrees up to 8 as the settled range and do not mention degree 9.
events.direction: Claims to confirm the conjecture for n = 9.

events.what_happened: Taboka Chalebgwa, 'Sendov's Conjecture: A note on a paper of Dégot' (arXiv 1804.09953, 26 Apr 2018, 19 pages). Derives an explicit N(a) for each a in (0,1) in Dégot's theorem and a uniform bound N for a in [α,β] with 0 < α < β < 1. The abstract says it 'partially addresses' Dégot's questions.
events.revisions: v1 only.
events.delivers: For zeros a in a closed subinterval [α,β] of (0,1), an explicit degree threshold beyond which a critical point lies within distance 1 of a.
events.remains: Zeros near 0 or near 1; degrees below the threshold; the full conjecture.
events.direction: Confirms the conjecture for a restricted class of zeros in high degree.

events.what_happened: Robert Dalmasso, 'On the Sendov conjecture for polynomials with simple zeros' (arXiv 1805.05681, 15 May 2018). The abstract says it 'gives a partial result when p has simple zeros.' The theorem was not stated on the abstract page.
events.revisions: v1 only.
events.delivers: A partial result for polynomials whose zeros are all simple; the exact class and degrees are not stated on the abstract page.
events.remains: Polynomials with repeated zeros; the full conjecture.
events.direction: Partial confirmation for simple zeros.

The arXiv v3 is marked withdrawn; v4 (5 Mar 2020) is the version shown. The critique (next event) names S. A. Shabir as co-author, while the arXiv listing names only G. M. Sofi.

events.remains: Nothing, if the claim held; the critique says it does not.
events.doubts: Rather and Gulzar's critique (arXiv 1903.04026, next event) says the proof 'is not correct'. The step the critique targets was not read in full.

events.what_happened: Theophilus Agama, 'Expansivity theory and Sendov's conjecture' (arXiv 1907.12825, 30 Jul 2019; v5 17 Mar 2026, 47 pages). The abstract says the paper proves 'some weak variants' of the conjecture and that 'As an application we give a proof of Sendov's conjecture.' The v5 comment says the paper was reformatted and its introduction expanded, 'ideas remains unchanged'.

events.what_happened: Terence Tao, 'Sendov's conjecture for sufficiently high degree polynomials' (arXiv 2012.04125, 8 Dec 2020; blog post 9 Dec 2020). Proves that there is an absolute constant n₀ such that the conjecture holds for all n ≥ n₀, with no explicit value. Published in Acta Mathematica 229(2): 347–392 (2022), DOI 10.4310/ACTA.2022.v229.n2.a3, per MathWorld and Wikipedia.
events.revisions: v1 8 Dec 2020; v2 31 May 2022 (comment 'To appear, Acta Mathematica').
events.delivers: Sendov for all degrees n ≥ n₀, for an unspecified absolute constant n₀. The method uses compactness, the argument principle and potential theory.
events.remains: Degrees 2 ≤ n < n₀. The constant n₀ is not explicit.
events.direction: Confirms the conjecture for all sufficiently large degrees, non-explicitly.

events.what_happened: Petar P. Petrov, 'Analyticity domains of critical points of polynomials. A proof of Sendov's conjecture' (arXiv 2104.00348, math.CV). The abstract says that the zeros and critical points of the second kind of certain polynomials depend analytically on the variables, and that 'This statement gives an immediate proof to the well-known conjecture of Bl. Sendov.' No journal reference on the abstract page.
events.revisions: v1 1 Apr 2021; v2 4 Apr 2021; v3 8 Apr 2021; v4 16 Apr 2021; v5 25 Nov 2021 (current).
events.delivers: Claims the full conjecture as an immediate consequence of an analyticity result for polynomials whose derivatives factor in a prescribed way (per the abstract).
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim held; no verification was found.
events.doubts: Drury and Lin (2022) say, in the full text of their paper (not opened in full; their abstract page does not mention Petrov), that the validity of Petrov's proof 'has not been confirmed yet'. No later confirmation or refutation was found.
events.direction: Claims to confirm the conjecture in full.

events.what_happened: Daebeom Choi and Seewoo Lee, 'Non-archimedean Sendov's Conjecture' (arXiv 2106.11155, 21 Jun 2021; v2 4 Jul 2021). The abstract claims a non-archimedean analogue and a complete list of polynomials over an algebraically closed non-archimedean field that meet the optimal bound. The page says nothing about the classical complex conjecture.
events.revisions: v1 21 Jun 2021; v2 4 Jul 2021 (adds a criterion for degree n with v(n) = 0).
events.delivers: An analogue over non-archimedean fields, not the complex statement. Discounted for this bullet.
events.remains: The classical complex conjecture, untouched.
events.direction: Analogue only; does not cut either way on the complex conjecture.

events.what_happened: K. Mahesh Krishna, 'C*-algebraic Gauss-Lucas Theorem and C*-algebraic Sendov's Conjecture' (arXiv 2203.06916, 14 Mar 2022). Formulates an operator-algebra analogue of Sendov's conjecture and verifies it only for polynomials of degree 2. The journal reference (Vestnik KRAUNC, 2026) is a later publication of the same work.
events.revisions: v1 only, submitted 14 Mar 2022; journal reference 2026, vol. 54, no. 1.
events.delivers: An analogue in unital commutative C*-algebras, verified for degree 2 only. Discounted for this bullet.
events.remains: The classical complex conjecture, untouched.

checked_by.what_they_did: published the paper in 2026 (per the abstract page's journal reference)

events.direction: Analogue only.

events.what_happened: Stephen Drury and Minghua Lin, 'Proof of Sendov's conjecture' (arXiv 2210.08720). v1 (17 Oct 2022) claimed a matrix-based proof; v2 (22 Oct 2022) is withdrawn by Minghua Lin, with the comment 'There is a gap in the proof. We are trying to fix it'. No PDF survives for v2.
events.revisions: v1 17 Oct 2022 (9 KB); v2 22 Oct 2022 (1 KB, withdrawn).
events.delivers: v1 claimed the full conjecture. The withdrawn v2 concedes a gap.
events.remains: Nothing, as withdrawn.
events.doubts: The author's own comment: 'There is a gap in the proof.' The gap is not identified in the abstract page or in v2.

withdrawn.what: v2 withdrawn by Minghua Lin, with the comment 'There is a gap in the proof. We are trying to fix it'

events.direction: Claimed full confirmation, conceded as incomplete.

events.what_happened: Robert Dalmasso, 'A result related to the Sendov conjecture' (arXiv 2309.07142, 5 Sep 2023; Annales Polonici Mathematici 2023, DOI 10.4064/ap221118-1-6). Asks whether, for a zero of multiplicity at least 2, there is a different critical point within distance 1 of it, and gives 'some partial results on the problem'. Read from the abstract page only.
events.revisions: v1 only.
events.delivers: Partial results on a related question for zeros of multiplicity at least 2; the specific theorems are not on the abstract page.
events.remains: The conjecture for simple zeros and in general.
events.direction: Partial results on a related question; not a resolution.

events.what_happened: Michael J. Miller, 'Seeking a quadratic refinement of Sendov's conjecture' (arXiv 2506.12951, 15 Jun 2025). Conjectures r(β) ≤ 1 − cβ(1 − β) for a constant c > 0 and all β in [0,1], which implies Sendov's bound r(β) ≤ 1 and, by rotation, covers all zeros. The abstract says the constants are found for complex polynomials of degree 2 and 3, real polynomials of degree 4, β near 1, polynomials with all roots on a line and polynomials with exactly one distinct critical point; numerical data suggest c ≈ 0.233.
events.revisions: v1 15 Jun 2025; v2 8 Sep 2025 (minor edits). Comments say it supersedes arXiv math/0312130.
events.delivers: Proves the refinement only in the listed classes: degree 2 (c₂ = 1/2), degree 3 (c₃ = 1/3), real degree 4, β near 1, polynomials with all roots on a line, and polynomials with exactly one distinct critical point. Within those classes this implies Sendov. The general refinement is conjectured.
events.remains: The general refinement for all polynomials and all β; Sendov for polynomials outside the listed classes.
events.direction: Stronger conjectured refinement; proven only in listed classes, which cut toward the bullet within those classes.

events.what_happened: Quanyu Tang and Teng Zhang, 'Sharp Schoenberg type inequalities and the de Bruin–Sharma problem' (arXiv 2508.10341, 14 Aug 2025). Confirms two conjectures of Georgiev, Gómez-Serrano, Tao and Wagner on order-4 Schoenberg-type inequalities, completing a solution of the de Bruin–Sharma problem, and derives sharp inequalities of orders −1 and −2m 'Motivated by Sendov's conjecture'. Section 5 contains identity (5.1) for normalised polynomials with nonzero zeros, and Remark 5.1 states that 'the case a=1 of Conjecture 1.9 (Sendov) follows directly from this identity'. Only the first part of the text (about 100k of 171k characters) and an excerpt of the rest were read.
events.revisions: v1 14 Aug 2025; v2 12 Nov 2025; v3 5 Dec 2025 (current).
events.delivers: Not a Sendov resolution. Its identity (5.1) gives the a = 1 case of Sendov's conjecture, the boundary case for zeros on the unit circle (see Remark 5.1), which is also the classical boundary case in Rubinstein's 1968 theorem. Other results concern Schoenberg-type inequalities.
events.remains: The conjecture for zeros with |a| < 1 and in general.
events.direction: Neighbouring inequality; by its own remark it contains the boundary case a = 1, which cuts toward the bullet in that case only.

events.what_happened: Fatima Amin Fneish, master's thesis on Sendov's conjecture at the American University of Beirut, defended 22 Aug 2025 per a search summary. Studies Tao's 2020 work and the existing theorems on zeros and critical points. Not opened: the AUB page returned HTTP 500.
events.delivers: Expository per the search summary; no new result claimed in what I could read.
events.remains: The conjecture.
events.direction: Expository; no bearing on the conjecture's truth.

events.what_happened: Beniamin Bogosel, 'Sendov's Conjecture and the Geometry of Cubic Polynomials', Theory and Applications of Mathematics and Computer Science 10(1), published 12 Dec 2025. The abstract says geometric arguments based on the Siebeck–Marden theorem 'prove Sendov's conjecture for cubic polynomials' and explore its sharpness. Any earlier preprint was not found; the date is the journal publication date.
events.revisions: Journal publication only as far as I found; no earlier preprint located.
events.delivers: Sendov for cubic polynomials, n = 3. This class was already covered by Rubinstein's 1968 theorem (interior zeros, n = 3), so the new content is a different proof.
events.remains: All degrees n ≥ 4.

checked_by.who: Theory and Applications of Mathematics and Computer Science (journal)

events.direction: Confirms the conjecture for cubic polynomials, a class already settled classically.

events.what_happened: Teng Zhang, 'Intersections of Convex Hulls of Polynomial Shifts and Critical Points' (arXiv 2601.16102, submitted 22 Jan 2026; withdrawn in v2, 25 Feb 2026). Claims a partial result toward Schmeisser's conjecture: if all zeros lie in the closed unit disk, then for every ζ in the convex hull K′ of the critical points, the disk |z − ζ| ≤ √(1 − |ζ|²) contains a critical point. The abstract does not mention Sendov. Schmeisser's conjecture is a different statement.
events.revisions: v1 22 Jan 2026; v2 25 Feb 2026, withdrawn.
events.delivers: Claims a partial result for a different, related conjecture (Schmeisser's). It is not a Sendov result. The withdrawn version's theorems are stated to be incorrect.
events.remains: Sendov's conjecture, untouched by this paper as far as the abstract shows.
events.doubts: The author's withdrawal comment: 'Theorems 1.2 and 2.5 in this paper are incorrect and the proofs also contain gaps.' The abstract's claimed results are therefore not established.

withdrawn.what: v2 withdrawn; comment: 'Theorems 1.2 and 2.5 in this paper are incorrect and the proofs also contain gaps.'

events.direction: Related problem only; claims withdrawn.

events.what_happened: Teng Zhang, 'Sendov's conjecture holds for every degree n ≥ 10^200000' (arXiv 2609.20256; 29 pages). Makes Tao's 2020/2022 existence result effective, with n₀ = 10^200000 (Theorem 1.2), by refining Tao's compactness-and-contradiction argument, its balayage and argument-principle steps, and the radius-selection mechanism of Tao's Theorem 3.1. The paper says 'The numerical bound in Theorem 1.2 can clearly be improved'. Read through the HTML full text in two chunks.
events.revisions: v1 only. The abstract page says 'Submitted on 28 Jul 2026', but the identifier 2609.20256 would normally indicate September 2026. The two disagree and I could not resolve it. The date recorded is the one the abstract page gives.
events.delivers: Sendov's conjecture for every degree n ≥ 10^200000. Does not depend on Mazur's 2026 proof, as far as the text shows (it never mentions Mazur).
events.remains: Every degree 2 ≤ n < 10^200000 is not covered by this event.
events.direction: Confirms the conjecture for all degrees at or above 10^200000.

events.what_happened: Lech Mazur posted a 'computer-assisted' proof of Sendov's conjecture for all degrees n ≥ 2 on ProofAtlas, a platform Mazur runs. The paper is titled 'A COMPUTER-ASSISTED PROOF OF SENDOV'S CONJECTURE' on the PDF and 'A Simplified Proof Candidate for Sendov's Conjecture' on the ProofAtlas research page, which calls it a 'proof candidate' and says it 'does not report an accepted resolution'. The author says GPT-5.6 Pro played a substantial role in its development. A Lean 4 package on ProofAtlas (1,160 first-party files, 92,816 lines, 'Unfinished proof steps: None', build reported as passed) accompanies it. I could not read the PDF (the fetch returned raw PDF data); the content here comes from the ProofAtlas HTML pages that describe it.
events.revisions: Public Revision 14 issued 2 Aug 2026 (release ID SENDOV-REV14-2026-08-02, per the ProofAtlas research page). The paper and public version are dated 5 Aug 2026 (ProofAtlas formalization page; Wikipedia references). Mazur's X pre-announcement 'Quick pre-announcement for people working on Sendov's conjecture: I posted a proof' is dated 3 Aug 2026 in the Wikipedia AI-discoveries list (the X post itself was not reachable). Revision 13 was the audited revision. A status note dated 19 Sep 2026 was added to the ProofAtlas formalization page and states that the archived manuscript is unchanged. I chose 2 Aug as the first public written argument, since Revision 14 is recorded as public on that date; the other dates are recorded here for the later pass.
events.delivers: Claims a complete proof of the full statement: for every complex polynomial p of degree n ≥ 2 with zeros in the closed unit disk and every zero a of p, a critical point lies within distance 1 of a. The page describes it as an 'all-degree, computer-assisted argument', with exact computation for the finite parts (16,862 finite certificate leaves, 20,994 exact rational boxes, 6,500 positive Bernstein coefficients) and 'two terminal scalar propositions' checked by exact programs. Restrictions per the author's pages: the earlier barrier reduction, product-defect bridge and other analytic steps are 'written mathematics only' (research page); 'No Lean or other proof-assistant formalization currently checks the manuscript's full argument' (research page); the Lean package is 'not a line-by-line formalization of the manuscript' and does not verify the supplementary Python programs (formalization page). Per Tao, the same argument also yields the Phelps–Rodriguez strengthening, which is outside this bullet.
events.remains: Nothing of the bullet, if the argument is accepted. The author's pages say the work has 'not yet received the independent specialist certification needed to present Sendov's conjecture as an established theorem', and ProofAtlas package acceptance is pending.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 with Mathlib (ProofAtlas package: 1,160 first-party files, 92,816 source lines, one recorded declaration in a 20-line Theorem.lean file)
machine_checked.note: The page says 'Unfinished proof steps: None' and 'Recorded build passed'. It also says the package is not a line-by-line formalization of the manuscript and does not verify the supplementary Python programs. The research page says no proof-assistant formalization currently checks the manuscript's full argument. The two pages are not consistent with each other on this point.

events.directly_checkable: The finite parts are exact certificates (16,862 leaves; 20,994 rational boxes; 6,500 positive Bernstein coefficients) produced by supplementary Python programs, which a reader can rerun. I did not read those programs. The informal steps are described as elementary by Tao (fundamental theorem of algebra, basic Möbius facts, a special case of Maclaurin's inequality).
events.doubts: (1) The author's own pages call the manuscript a 'proof candidate' and say specialist certification is pending. (2) Per the research page, the barrier reduction and product-defect bridge remain 'written mathematics only' and are not formalised. (3) The Lean package is not a line-by-line formalization of the manuscript. (4) The argument depends on exact computation for finite parts; the mid-range is the part the later work (An) tries to reduce. (5) The 19 Sep 2026 note says the ranking review 'records the mathematical target as resolved', but the page's own 'current status' section still says the result is not established; the two conflict. (6) Attribution is disputed in the Tao blog comments ('Lech Mazur with help of LLM' versus 'LLM+'; 'Humans lead this project, and humans deserve to be the author'). These are attribution objections, not objections to the mathematics. One commenter wrote that 'LM seems to only partially understand what he is doing'; that is an opinion, not an identified error.
events.direction: Confirms (proves) the conjecture for all degrees n ≥ 2, the direction the bullet asserts.
people: Lech Mazur (sole named author; takes responsibility for the manuscript)

systems.what_it_did: Per the author's ProofAtlas research page: GPT-5.6 Pro 'played a substantial role in mathematical exploration, proof development, computational testing, adversarial auditing, and exposition, with human orchestration, selection, and reconciliation of the resulting work'. The formalization page lists it as a development contributor that 'contributed to exploration, proof development, exact computational testing' and credits Mazur as 'accountable curator, workflow designer, and reconciler of model outputs'. Tao's blog calls the argument 'the AI-generated proof' and quotes Mazur as saying he 'was able to use an AI tool to resolve Sendov's conjecture for all n ≥ 2'. Tao's blog does not name the model. The model name comes from Mazur's pages.

events.what_happened: Terence Tao, 'A digestion of the proof of Sendov's conjecture' (blog, URL dated 12 Aug 2026). A human-readable reconstruction of Mazur's argument. It uses the fundamental theorem of algebra, basic facts about Möbius maps, and a special case of Maclaurin's inequality (derived from AM–HM and induction). It says the argument 'demonstrates Conjecture 3, and thus resolves both the Sendov conjecture and the Phelps–Rodriguez conjecture in full generality'. It gives a separate Hölder argument for n ≤ 4. It says that medium-range degrees 5 ≤ n ≤ 200 'require a certain amount of computer assistance', supported by a numerical applet and a Lean check of the bound. It says 'Here we use an AI-generated argument' for one polar inequality, and that some pieces were 'extracted from the AI proof with considerable effort'. It says the digest took 'several days (with heavy AI assistance)'. It also says the argument yields a new proof of Rubinstein's theorem. Read in full across three chunks.
events.revisions: Blog post dated 12 Aug 2026 by URL (Wikipedia list and MathWorld give 12 Aug; a remio.ai article gives 13 Aug in its URL). The comment thread continues with Tao's corrections (for example, the attribution of the Tang–Zhang identity, '[Corrected, thanks – T.]').
events.delivers: A human-readable argument that establishes the full Sendov statement for all n ≥ 2, by the mathematics of Mazur's argument, with the restrictions Tao states: n ≤ 4 by a separate elementary argument; 5 ≤ n ≤ 200 with computer assistance (numerical applet and Lean check of the bound); the remaining degrees by the argument. Also states the Phelps–Rodriguez strengthening, which is outside this bullet.
events.remains: No part of the bullet, per Tao's account, subject to the computer-assisted mid-range. Phelps–Rodriguez is outside this bullet.

checked_by.qualification: professional mathematician, author of arXiv:2012.04125 on this problem; the digest is an expert reconstruction, not a referee report

machine_checked.note: Only the two statements in Challenge.lean are unproved, by design. The audit script forbids sorry elsewhere. Axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. Builds against Lean toolchains v4.33.1 to v4.35.0 per Reservoir.

events.directly_checkable: The elementary steps (fundamental theorem of algebra, Möbius maps, Maclaurin special case via AM–HM and induction) are stated in the post for a reader to check by hand. The mid-range 5 ≤ n ≤ 200 is checked by a numerical applet and a Lean check of the bound.
events.doubts: (1) The mid-range depends on computer checks; the design document of the Lean repository records a seam inconsistency (the text says n ≥ 98 is handled analytically, but the implemented split is at 100/101). (2) The post says that some steps are the AI's, and that the AI-generated proof was not digested into publication form. (3) A commenter objects to credit ('Lech Mazur with help of LLM' versus 'LLM+'). (4) The post and the Lean repository do not claim independent review; the repository says 'No external or independent review has been performed'.

events.what_happened: Lean 4 formalization of Sendov's and the Phelps–Rodriguez conjecture in the repository github.com/teorth/sendov (Reservoir package 'sendov' 0.1.0, Apache-2.0). Main theorems Sendov.sendov and Sendov.phelps_rodriguez. The statement of record is Challenge.lean (87 lines, importing only Mathlib). The Sendov statement: for p in ℂ[X] with natDegree n, 2 ≤ n, all roots in the closed disk, and p(a) = 0, there is ζ with p′(ζ) = 0 and ‖ζ − a‖ ≤ 1. The README says the mathematics 'descends from Lech Mazur's proof' and 'No novelty is claimed anywhere in this repository'. The repository was built in a session on 10–13 Aug 2026 (making-of), and Reservoir records the last update as 31 Aug 2026.
events.revisions: Reservoir: package last updated 31 Aug 2026; GitHub: 64 commits, no commit date read. The making-of records development on 10–13 Aug 2026 in one long session, compacted several times.
events.delivers: A machine check that the stated theorems hold, with the formal statement matching the classical wording: n ≥ 2, closed disk, distance ≤ 1, critical point as a zero of p′. Reservoir lists 80 files and 15,152 lines. The design document records a finite-range check for 5 ≤ n ≤ 100 (Bernstein certificates from untrusted Python generators, re-checked in Lean with ring) and an analytic route for n ≥ 101. The statement is the Lean reading of the problem; the mathematics is Tao's digest of Mazur's argument.
events.remains: Nothing of the statement. The match between the Lean statement and the classical problem is for human reading.
events.time_since_posted: about 6 weeks since the last update (31 Aug 2026)

machine_checked.note: The audit script allows exactly the two statements in Challenge.lean to be unproved. No native_decide, unsafe or floating point. Axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. Reservoir records builds against v4.33.1 to v4.35.0 and says build data for v4.35.0 is on the repository CI.

events.directly_checkable: Challenge.lean (the statement of record) can be read against the classical statement. Certificates are produced by untrusted Python scripts and re-checked in Lean. The design document says a clean rebuild from a fresh clone is still listed as remaining work (§7).
events.doubts: (1) The README says 'No external or independent review has been performed.' (2) The design document is internally inconsistent: §6b says the complex-analytic derivation of two raw inequalities remains outside Lean, while §6c and the status table say those files are proved. The seam between finite and large-degree ranges is stated as n ≥ 98 but implemented at 100/101. (3) The making-of document says Claude twice wrote sorry placeholders and removed them before committing, reporting the lapses. (4) Building all 31 batch files at once runs out of memory. (5) The making-of document says a 'Palomar registry' accepted the submission with a reviewer comment that novelty claims lacked a documented literature search. I did not verify this registry or identify the reviewer.

events.what_happened: Senjian An, 'A Scalar Optimization Proof of Sendov's Conjecture with Reduced Computer Assistance' (arXiv 2609.04246, 22 Aug 2026; v1 only). Builds on 'Mazur's recent proof, and Tao's streamlined exposition of it', which reduces a hypothetical counterexample to a scalar lower bound. The paper imports the bound on α from Tao's exposition (Proposition 11(ii)) and reduces the remaining computations to a finite certificate over 34 half-unit slabs covering α ∈ (0,17], giving a bound 97/100 < 1 that contradicts the scalar lower bound. The paper states Theorem 1.1 for every n ≥ 2 but says the classical low-degree arguments cover n ≤ 5, which it does not reprove, so the new argument handles n ≥ 6 given the Mazur–Tao reduction.
events.revisions: v1 only (22 Aug 2026, 35 KB, per the abstract page). The identifier 2609.04246 would normally denote September 2026, so the listed date and the identifier disagree.
events.delivers: A reduction of the computer assistance in the Mazur–Tao scalar step, conditional on that step and on the imported α bound, giving the n ≥ 6 case. Not an independent proof of the full statement.
events.remains: The imported α bound (Tao's Proposition 11(ii)) and the Mazur–Tao reduction are inputs, not proved here. The 34-slab certificate is computer-checked, not formal. Degrees n ≤ 5 are not reproved here.

checked_by.qualification: not established from the paper's abstract or declarations
checked_by.what_they_did: re-argued the scalar step with a two-stage optimisation and a finite certificate; acknowledges Mazur for the proof architecture and Tao for the streamlined scalar reduction

events.directly_checkable: The 34-slab certificate and the explicit one-variable inequalities can be recomputed by a reader. The paper's code was not read.
events.doubts: (1) It depends on Tao's Proposition 11(ii) and on the Mazur–Tao reduction, neither proved in this paper. (2) The computer assistance is confined to a finite certificate but not removed. (3) The paper's own declaration says 'No language-model output is treated as mathematical evidence', so the certificate is the only check offered. (4) Single version; no review found.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture for n ≥ 6, conditional on the Mazur–Tao reduction.
events.object: No polynomial counterexample. The paper excludes a hypothetical counterexample by a finite numerical certificate (34 half-unit α-slabs; bound 97/100 < 1) together with explicit one-variable inequalities.

systems.name: OpenAI’s ChatGPT, including GPT-5-series models used during 2026

The architecture-proposal role may be load-bearing under §5.4; the paper does not say which architecture it was. The Lean checks of auxiliary identities are not described as part of the result.

events.what_happened: Teng Zhang, 'Beyond Sendov's conjecture: the quadratic Tang–Zhang inequality' (arXiv 2609.19126, 16 Sep 2026; 839 KB, v1 only). Proves for a polynomial of degree n ≥ 2 with zeros in the closed unit disk and critical points ζ_1…ζ_{n−1} counted with multiplicity, that every zero a satisfies Σ_j 1/|a − ζ_j|² ≥ n − 1, with equality exactly for p(z) = c(z^n − ω), c ≠ 0 and |ω| = 1. The abstract says 'Lech Mazur proved the celebrated Sendov conjecture' and that Tao 'distilled the main ideas of the proof in a blog post'. The paper follows Tao's reciprocal coordinates and identities and says its polar argument is 'closely related to the small-degree arguments in [Maz26]'. The Lean 4 formalization 'of the quadratic Tang–Zhang inequality' is listed in the bibliography, with Lean v4.34.0-rc1, but no URL was given in what I read.
events.revisions: v1 only (submitted 16 Sep 2026).
events.delivers: A quantitative strengthening of Sendov's conjecture. The inequality implies Sendov: if the sum of n − 1 terms 1/|a − ζ_j|² is at least n − 1, some term is at least 1, so some critical point lies within distance 1 of a. The paper states it as a theorem, not a conjecture. The paper's own account says its mathematical arguments were 'independently developed, checked, and written by the author', but it builds on Tao's identities, so independence from Mazur's route is not established.
events.remains: The bullet itself is not separately established here; the result is a stronger inequality that gives it, if the inequality's proof holds.
events.doubts: Only the abstract and the first 100k characters of the text (of 106k) were read; the proof of the inequality was not checked. The Lean formalization is claimed without a URL and its sorry status is not established, so machine_checked is left null.
events.direction: Strengthens and implies the bullet.
events.object: Equality cases: p(z) = c(z^n − ω) with |ω| = 1 (the same extremal family as for the constant 1 in the bullet).

The same disclosure says ChatGPT was used for 'English-language editing, proofreading, grammatical corrections', and that 'The mathematical arguments and proofs in the original manuscript were independently developed, checked, and written by the author.' The Codex role is a formalisation role; whether it belongs in the result is for the later pass.

disputes.summary: The Lean README credits the underlying mathematics to Lech Mazur's proof and says 'No novelty is claimed anywhere in this repository'. Tao's digest credits Mazur with the AI-assisted proof. The Zhang paper says Mazur 'proved the celebrated Sendov conjecture'. No dispute over priority for the all-degree proof is visible in the sources I read, but one commenter on Tao's blog objects to the attribution ('Lech Mazur with help of LLM' versus 'LLM+'), and another says 'Humans lead this project, and humans deserve to be the author'.

The boundary identity (the a = 1 case) appears in Tang and Zhang (2025, Remark 5.1), and the Lean package credits the identity to Tang and Zhang and the classification to Rubinstein (1968). Tao's digest says it yields 'a new proof of Rubinstein's theorem'. The Lean README says no novelty is claimed for the boundary argument.

Earlier claimed full proofs by Schmieder (2002–03), Sofi (2019), Agama (2019), Petrov (2021) and Drury–Lin (2022) all predate the 2026 claim. Sofi's and Drury–Lin's claims are refuted or withdrawn; the others were not confirmed or refuted in the sources I read. Each is recorded as its own event.

Dates and line counts disagree across sources. The first public version is 2 Aug (ProofAtlas revision log), 3 Aug (Mazur's X pre-announcement, per the Wikipedia AI list) or 5 Aug (PDF, public version, and Wikipedia). The Lean package is 92,816 lines (ProofAtlas, Mazur's package) or 15,152 lines (Tao's streamlined repository), and both are reported in the same sources. Wikipedia's article dates Sendov's posing to 1959, and other sources say 1958.

The listed arXiv dates and identifiers disagree for three papers: 2609.20256 is listed as submitted 28 Jul 2026 (its identifier would normally be September); 2609.04246 is listed as 22 Aug 2026 (its identifier would normally be August); 2609.19126 is listed as 16 Sep 2026 (consistent). I recorded the listed dates and did not resolve the conflict.

summary: The problem has moved since January 2024, and the largest move is the August 2026 claim of a full proof. The claim, by Lech Mazur on ProofAtlas, was generated with OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro according to the author's own pages (the first public version is recorded as 2 Aug 2026, with 3 and 5 Aug also reported; I chose 2 Aug because the ProofAtlas revision log records a public Revision 14 on that date, and the other dates are kept in the event's revisions field). Tao digested the argument on 12 Aug 2026 and states that it establishes the full statement for all n ≥ 2, using elementary tools for n ≥ 5 except for computer assistance over 5 ≤ n ≤ 200, and that it also gives the Phelps–Rodriguez strengthening, which is outside this bullet. A Lean 4 formalization of Tao's version (teorth/sendov) states the theorem, uses only the standard axioms and leaves only the statement file unproved by design. The repository's README says Claude Opus 5 wrote essentially all of the Lean source, and Tao's digest says the Lean formalization was produced 'with an AI agent'. Two later preprints build on the result: Senjian An (2609.04246) reduces the computer assistance in the scalar step, and Teng Zhang (2609.19126) proves a stronger inequality that implies the bullet. Teng Zhang's large-degree result (2609.20256, n ≥ 10^200000) predates the Mazur claim in its listed date, but it covers only very large degrees. Against the claim: the author's ProofAtlas pages call it a 'proof candidate' with independent specialist certification pending, its analytic steps are 'written mathematics only' per the research page, the Lean package is not a line-by-line formalization of the manuscript, the repository states 'No external or independent review has been performed', and I found no named expert referee report. Earlier claims (Schmieder 2002–03, Sofi 2019 refuted by Rather–Gulzar, Agama 2019, Petrov 2021, Drury–Lin 2022 withdrawn with an author-stated gap) were not confirmed. The close calls are: (1) which date is the first public written argument; (2) whether Tao's digest is a separate event or the same mathematics, and I recorded it separately; (3) whether Lean formalisation by Claude Opus 5 and Codex is AI 'in the result', since the Claude entry includes lemma-level proofs (Maclaurin's inequality, a defect lemma, a sinh bound) that the making-of document calls mathematical content; (4) whether the Tang–Zhang boundary identity counts as new, since the Lean package credits it to Tang and Zhang and attributes the classification to Rubinstein (1968); and (5) whether the 2609.20256 and 2609.04246 dates, which conflict with their identifiers, should be trusted. Non-AI computer assistance: exact certificates in Mazur's pages, numerical applets and Lean-checked bounds in Tao's mid-range, and a 34-slab certificate in An's paper are computer-assisted but are not AI systems. The AI declarations in Zhang (2609.20256) name DeepSeek for language editing and literature searches, and in Zhang (2609.19126) name ChatGPT for editing; neither is in the result and neither is in ai.systems. Two other items are noted but not recorded as events: a 2025 TAMCS paper (Bogosel) proves the cubic case, which Rubinstein already covered classically, and Miller's 2025 refinement is conjectural with partial proofs in listed classes. Searches for AI involvement beyond these (Aristotle, AlphaProof, Gemini Deep Think, Quanta) found nothing relevant for this problem.
competing_reading: The strongest case that this is settled: the all-degree argument is a machine-checked theorem in Lean 4 (teorth/sendov, standard axioms, only the statement file unproved by design), Tao has digested it into an elementary human-readable argument, two independent later papers build on it, and Wikipedia describes it as a proof. On this reading, the 'proof candidate' label on ProofAtlas is a stale or cautious wording, and the Lean check is the decisive evidence. The strongest case the other way: the author's own pages say the manuscript is a proof candidate with specialist certification pending; the Lean package is not a line-by-line formalization of the manuscript and the analytic steps are described as written mathematics only; the mid-range depends on computer certificates (in Tao's digest, Mazur's pages and An's paper); the repository states no external review; Tao's digest describes the AI argument as not publication-ready; and the Tang–Zhang identity used for the boundary is itself a 2025 preprint without journal review. On the AI question, the authors' own accounts make the GPT-5.6 Pro argument the substance of the proof (load-bearing on the authors' own account), while the other reading is that Mazur curated and reconciled it and that the human-led Tao digest, and not the AI's output, is what gives the statement its present form.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A named specialist's written verification of Mazur's manuscript or of Tao's digest, or journal acceptance; (2) the ProofAtlas accepted-result review's outcome, pending as of the pages I read; (3) an independent Lean build from a fresh clone of teorth/sendov, plus a reading of Challenge.lean against the classical statement (the design document lists the fresh-clone rebuild as remaining work); (4) the true first-public date of the Mazur manuscript, from ProofAtlas's revision log or a public timestamp; (5) reading the Mazur PDF itself (the fetch returned raw PDF data) to confirm the AI-role wording and the computational claims; (6) the correct arXiv dates for 2609.20256 and 2609.04246, which conflict with their identifiers; (7) an independent check of An's 34-slab certificate and the imported α bound; (8) for the Zhang inequality (2609.19126), the full text beyond the first 100k characters and the Lean URL.
